extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners assessing inter-rater agreement (psychologists, clinicians, statisticians, psychometricians)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and interpretations for using Cohen's kappa to summarize and interpret nominal-scale inter-rater agreement, including algebraic interpretations, pitfalls, and recommended reporting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kappa as a function of the proportion of observed and expected agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohen's kappa is defined as a function of the observed agreement P_o and the expected agreement P_e: κ = (P_o − P_e) / (1 − P_e). Here P_o = sum of p_ii (proportion of subjects classified into the same category by both raters) and P_e = sum of p_i+ * p_+i (base-rate product sums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the usual formula found in introductory statistics textbooks; compute P_o from diagonal cell proportions and P_e from marginal base rates. Example calculations are given for three example tables (Table 1: κ = 0.75; Table 2: κ = 0.85; Table 3: κ = 0.91).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kappa as the proportion of agreement corrected for chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa can be interpreted as the proportion of observed agreement corrected for chance: a chance-corrected measure M has the form (M − E(M))/(1 − E(M)), and for M = P_o this yields κ. Kappa has value zero under statistical independence of the raters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation motivates why kappa is preferred to raw observed agreement when independence (chance agreement) would inflate agreement. Compute using κ = (P_o − P_e)/(1 − P_e). Emphasize that a coefficient with nonzero value under independence can be misleading; kappa's zero-under-independence property is desirable for chance correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on base rates (prevalence) affects comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa depends on the base rates of the categories (how often categories are used by the raters); kappas from samples with different base rates are therefore not comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious comparing kappa values across samples with different marginal distributions. The article cites literature identifying difficulties with interpretation due to base-rate dependence and warns that kappa's value can change solely because of prevalence differences rather than true agreement differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kappa as the average kappa when two categories are combined
rubrics_metrics.description: With m categories there are m(m−1)/2 ways to combine two categories; the overall kappa is a weighted average of the kappas obtained when combining each possible pair of categories (weights are the denominators of the individual kappas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining categories can either increase or decrease kappa (contrary to common misconception). Examples from Table 1 show κ changes (e.g., combining categories 1 and 2 decreased κ from 0.75 to 0.17, whereas combining 3 and 4 increased κ to 0.82). If combining categories in practice, consider the substantive meaning of the new category. Weights for the average are given (example weights: 0.63, 0.61, 0.63, 0.62, 0.64, 0.62) and the weighted average equals the overall κ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kappa as the average category reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa can be viewed as an average of category-specific reliabilities: for each category i, the category reliability κ_i is the kappa computed on a 2×2 table where category i is contrasted with ‘all others’; the overall κ is a weighted average of these κ_i (weights are the denominators of the κ_i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both overall kappa and individual category reliabilities because the overall single number can mask heterogeneity across categories (example: κ_1 = 0.89 vs κ_3 = 0.67 for Table 1). The article provides example category reliabilities and their weights (e.g., weights 0.19, 0.18, 0.20, 0.18 giving overall κ = 0.75).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kappa as an intraclass correlation (ICC) via variance partitioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Using Gini–Light–Margolin partitioning for qualitative data, Cohen's kappa may be expressed in variance-component form akin to an intraclass correlation: κ = (σ_s^2 − σ_e^2 / N) / (σ_r^2 + σ_s^2 + σ_e^2 / N) (equation given), which for large N approximates an ICC that includes systematic rater variability as part of total variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation links kappa to familiar variance-based reliability concepts (ICC). It allows interpretation of κ as the degree of resemblance of subjects (in terms of variance structure). Use when conceptualizing reliability in variance-component terms or when comparing with ICCs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landis and Koch interpretive benchmarks (conventional labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common guideline labels for kappa values: 0.00–0.20 indicates slight agreement, 0.21–0.40 fair agreement, 0.41–0.60 moderate agreement, 0.61–0.80 substantial agreement, and 0.81–1.00 almost perfect agreement (Landis & Koch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These benchmarks are frequently used but should be treated as arbitrary; the article explicitly notes they are generally considered arbitrary and should not be applied uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate kappa variant and be aware of extensions/limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many extensions of Cohen's kappa, including kappas for three or more raters, kappas for ordinal categories, and weighted kappas; Cohen's original κ (equation (3)) remains widely used but may be inappropriate for other data structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a kappa variant that matches the number of raters and measurement level (e.g., use multi-rater kappa for >2 raters, weighted kappa for ordinal data). Be aware of known paradoxes and inequalities in kappa behavior cited in the literature; consult referenced literature for alternatives and special cases.
